changes.before: Add request validation, authorization, middleware, and failure handling.
changes.after: Change a record only after identity, ownership, and input checks pass.

before: Authentication asks who is signed in. Authorization asks whether that person may act on a particular record. Validation asks whether the proposed values are acceptable. A protected update needs all three. Being signed in does not grant access to someone else's record, and owning a record does not make an invalid duration acceptable.

The order makes the write safe. Return before assignment whenever a requirement fails. A request body can claim ownerId: 'nora', but anyone can submit that text. The trusted identity must come from a server-verified session, then be compared with the record's stored owner. The permission helper accepts that verified result; it must not be treated as proof that an arbitrary supplied object really represents a signed-in person.

A session is a server-recognized sign-in state. In a real flow, the server verifies credentials, issues an unpredictable token, and checks that token and its expiry on later requests. A cookie can carry the token. The browser's claim to be a user is not trusted without that verification. Middleware runs before the route, validates the session, and attaches a trusted identity such as req.user; the route then performs record-specific authorization.

For the exercise, authorizeUpdate receives verified-session fixtures and mutates entry.minutes only after all checks pass. Null session returns 401; mismatched ownership returns 403; invalid minutes returns 400; a valid owner update returns 200 with entry. True AND false AND true is false: valid sign-in and input cannot overcome failed ownership. To finish actual protection locally, connect real session verification before using this helper; the next full-stack project supplies a localhost sign-in flow.
after: A protected update needs three things: a verified identity, permission to change this record, and valid new data. Passing one check does not make up for failing another.

Check the session before reading its userId. Compare that ID with the record's stored ownerId. Return immediately when a check fails, before assigning entry.minutes. A caller's ownerId claim in the request body is not proof of ownership.
Even the owner must supply whole-number minutes from 1 through 180. Invalid minutes return 400 and leave the record unchanged. A valid owner update changes minutes and returns 200 with the entry.

A real server must verify the sign-in, recognize its session token, and check expiry before supplying the identity. This helper does none of that. Its simple session objects are practice inputs, not a working authentication system.

Middleware is code that runs before the route handler. It can reject an invalid session or pass a trusted identity to the route. In Express, next() continues to later code. Return after sending a rejection so that later writing code does not run.

Complete authorizeUpdate in this order: no session gives 401, wrong owner gives 403, and invalid minutes gives 400. Only then assign minutes and return 200 with entry. Check that every rejected call preserves the original record.

before: Write authorizeUpdate. Return 401 when there is no session.
Return 403 when the signed-in user does not own the record.
Return 400 unless minutes is a whole number from 1 to 180. Return 200 when the update is allowed.
If an update is refused, leave the original record unchanged.
Optional follow-on after the next full-stack lesson: in your local Express route, verify the session before running this permission check.
Never use req.body.ownerId as proof of who the user is.

Optional follow-on with that local app: test no session, the wrong owner, boundary values, and a valid owner update. The current browser exercise tests the permission helper with verified-session fixtures.
after: Check the verified session and stored ownership.
Update only after every check passes.
Check both returned statuses and unchanged data after rejection.

before: Check for a session before reading session.userId.
Compare session.userId with entry.ownerId before changing entry.
Return immediately on every failed check, then update only the permitted record.
after: Return immediately after each failed check.
Never use the request body's ownerId to establish identity.
Check the record after a rejected update.

before.question: Which source should a protected route trust to learn who the user is?
choices: user ID from a verified server session
the first record in the database
before.explanation: The server must verify the session and then compare that identity with record ownership.

after.question: What should a protected route use to learn who the caller is?
choices: The user ID from a verified server session
after.explanation: The server verifies the session, then uses that trusted identity for the permission check.

changes.before: This project checks permission logic with verified-session fixtures. In your local server, provide real sign-in and session validation before using it. The next full-stack project supplies a local sign-in flow; fixtures are not authentication.
changes.after: The browser tests this permission helper with supplied, verified-session examples. A real server must perform sign-in and session verification before calling it.

headings: Verify the session on the server

project.title: A protected practice API
project.task: Complete authorizeUpdate with identity, ownership, and minutes checks before any write. Return the specified status for each result.
project.done_when: Rejected requests leave the record unchanged; a valid owner update changes only the permitted record.
